title: Skincare Spa and Clinic Management
desc: Plan and run a small skincare spa or clinic: services, hygiene, consent, scheduling, products, pricing and client care.
outcomes: Explain service menus, scope of practice and hygiene rules.
Run client intake, consent and patch-test steps.
Build a schedule and cost per treatment.
Judge product claims and ingredient labels.
Launch a 30-day pilot with a client-care review.
task: Plan and pilot a small skincare spa service menu with hygiene plan, consent forms, pricing, schedule and client feedback log.
condition: A practice room or real licensed space, a spreadsheet, two peers and a licensed practitioner as mentor. Medical treatments are outside scope.
standard: Hygiene checklist passes; every service has a scope note; costs and price are shown; consent and patch-test steps are recorded; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Beauty therapists, spa owners, front-desk staff, small clinic managers.
evidence: service menu, hygiene plan, intake and consent forms, price sheet, pilot log
modules: Service menu and scope of practice
Understand
A spa must offer only what its staff are trained and allowed to do.
Typical services: cleansing facials, light exfoliation, massage, relaxation treatments.
Medical or invasive treatments belong with a doctor.
Write who may perform each service and what training they need.
Refer any skin change, lump or bleeding mole to a doctor.
A spa lists facials and body massage but writes "we do not treat medical skin conditions; we refer to a doctor". A client with a changing mole is referred the same day.
Write a menu of eight services with duration, scope note and qualification needed.
Each service has a qualification note and a referral line.
Hygiene and infection control
Apply
Clean practice protects clients and the business.
Wash hands before and after each client; use clean towels and single-use items.
Clean and sterilise tools by a stated method and cycle; log it.
Clean surfaces between clients; manage waste safely.
Check the room at the start and end of each day.
A tool tray is cleaned, sterilised for the full cycle, dried and stored covered. The log records date, time and initials.
Write a hygiene checklist and a daily log sheet.
Every step has a time and an initials box.
Client intake, consent and patch tests
Apply
Know the client before touching skin.
Ask about allergies, medicines, pregnancy, skin conditions and recent procedures.
Do a patch test 24 to 48 hours before a new product where advised.
Obtain written consent and explain aftercare.
Store records securely.
A client reports a nut allergy. The therapist avoids a nut-oil product, records the allergy on the card and chooses a different oil.
Design an intake and consent form and fill it for a practice client.
Form covers allergy, medicine, pregnancy, consent and patch test result.
Products and ingredients
Evaluate
Choose products on evidence, not on promises.
Read ingredient lists; know common allergens and irritants.
Reject miracle claims and unproven treatments.
Check storage, opening dates and expiry.
Buy from reliable suppliers with batch information.
A cream lists fragrance as the first ingredient. The therapist avoids it for sensitive skin and chooses a fragrance-free option.
Review three product labels and write a safety note for each.
Each note names allergens and storage rules.
Scheduling and capacity
Analyse
Time is the main resource.
Room time = service time + cleaning + buffer.
Match staff and rooms to peak times.
Use online booking with reminders.
Track late cancellations and no-shows.
A 60-minute facial needs 80 minutes of room time. Two rooms and two staff can deliver 6 facials in an 8-hour day, not 8.
Build a one-day schedule for two staff and two rooms.
No overlaps and cleaning time shown.
Pricing and profit
Evaluate
Price must cover cost and leave a margin.
Costs: staff time, products, rent share, laundry, booking fees, insurance.
Price = cost + margin; check against local prices.
Packages and loyalty rewards must remain profitable.
Review prices every quarter.
A facial costs 520 INR to deliver and sells at 1,100 INR, giving 580 INR margin. A 10% package discount still leaves 480 INR.
Cost five services and set prices with currency shown.
Totals correct and margin shown for each.
Client care and reactions
Apply
Calm, kind service builds trust, and a clear protocol handles problems.
Greet, explain, check comfort, give aftercare tips.
If a reaction occurs: stop, rinse, cool, record, advise medical help if needed.
Handle complaints politely and record them.
Follow up with clients after treatments.
A client reports redness. Staff stop the treatment, cool the skin, record the product used and call the mentor, who advises a doctor visit. The incident is logged.
Write a reaction protocol and role-play it.
Steps are in order and contact numbers listed.
Pilot and improve
Create
Run 30 days of real service and learn from the numbers.
Track bookings, rebookings, complaints and product waste.
Fix the top three issues.
Plan fair pay and responsible disposal.
Collect client feedback.
Rebooking rises from 32% to 45% after aftercare cards. Product waste falls 12% with smaller sample sizes.
Present the pilot review.
Numbers are real and three fixes are dated.
quiz: Why list scope?
To keep to training and licence. (Covered in module 1: Service menu and scope of practice. To pass that module: Each service has a qualification note and a referral line.)
Name two hygiene steps.
Hand washing and sterilising tools. (Covered in module 2: Hygiene and infection control. To pass that module: Every step has a time and an initials box.)
What is a patch test?

A small test on skin before a full treatment. (Covered in module 3: Client intake, consent and patch tests. To pass that module: Form covers allergy, medicine, pregnancy, consent and patch test result.)
Name a common allergen.
Fragrance or nut oil. (Covered in module 4: Products and ingredients. To pass that module: Each note names allergens and storage rules.)
What to do on a reaction?
Stop, rinse, record, get medical help if needed. (Covered in module 5: Scheduling and capacity. To pass that module: No overlaps and cleaning time shown.)
What is room time?
Service plus cleaning and buffer. (Covered in module 6: Pricing and profit. To pass that module: Totals correct and margin shown for each.)
What costs go into a price?
Staff, products, rent share, laundry, fees. (Covered in module 7: Client care and reactions. To pass that module: Steps are in order and contact numbers listed.)
Why miracle claims bad?
They mislead and break rules. (Covered in module 8: Pilot and improve. To pass that module: Numbers are real and three fixes are dated.)
What do you track in a pilot?
Bookings, rebooks, complaints, waste. (Covered in module 8: Pilot and improve. To pass that module: Numbers are real and three fixes are dated.)
When refer to a doctor?
Skin changes or medical concerns. (Covered in module 8: Pilot and improve. To pass that module: Numbers are real and three fixes are dated.)
rubric: Every claim linked to a dated record and checked by a peer
Checked, dated and explained to others
